newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Students jeer Berisha, Shkoder backs hunger strike.
newsitem.headline: Students jeer Berisha, Shkoder backs hunger strike.

text.p: Students in southern Albania jeered President Sali Berisha on Wednesday after he rejected their demands for the government to resign and reimburse investors for money lost in a savings scandal.

The president, who must seek a fresh term of office by March 9, took time out of his schedule during a visit to Gjirokaster to meet some 700 university students who have called an indefinite boycott of classes in protest at the government's handling of failed pyramid investment schemes.
Berisha said the government bore some blame for failing to warn investors about the scams in time but the main responsibility lay with gullible investors.
"I cannot support the illegitimate request to reimburse money...(But) as a physician, I would not allow anyone to die from a hunger strike," Berisha told the students.

Students in Albania's southernmost town of Gjirokaster, near the Greek border, said they were boycotting classes indefinitely in solidarity with students on hunger strike in the southern town of Vlore.
The Vlore student hunger strike appeared to be an increasing focus of anti-government resentment over the financial scandal.

Three buses and cars carrying some 120 people from the northern city of Shkoder, including rightist mayor Bahri Borici, travelled the 260 km (170 miles) to Vlore on Wednesday to express support for the hunger strikers.
"The students' request are right. We are for a political solution and then an economic one," Borici told reporters.
Supporters from other towns, including Durres, Kavaje and Fier joined around 7,000 people for a daily peaceful demonstration running for the past three weeks.
Tirana students have also voiced backing for Vlore students but police have prevented them from holding any demonstrations.
Apart from Tirana, the south is the most prosperous region in Europe's poorest state and it was badly hit by the collapse of two pyramid schemes favoured by thousands of people.
The most violent clashes hit Vlore two weeks ago when one man was shot dead and two others died of heart attacks.
Speaking to a rally of some 1,500 supporters at Gjirokaster sports hall, Berisha pledged to create a free trade zone in the area, more social assistance and credits for small businesses.
In Tirana, the Forum for Democracy grouping 15 opposition parties and other groups said it opposed Berisha's re-election, saying it would only deepen the crisis in the country.
Parliament elects the president and Berisha is sure to win a fresh five-year mandate with his right-wing Democrats holding 122 of 140 seats after last year's disputed general election.
The Forum also complained that police were preventing them from holding peaceful protests, a measure criticised by the U.S. State Department on Tuesday.
The State Department called on Tirana to draw up a new constitution and hold fresh elections but Berisha brushed aside the appeal.
"There will be no early elections. Elections will be held in 2000," Berisha told cheering supporters in Gjirokaster.
